planting.note: Pot up rooted plants only after nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55F, since cold, wet soil quickly rots the swollen caudex.

directions: This Madagascar endemic forms a smooth, swollen grey caudex topped with a crown of narrow, glossy leaves and, unlike its taller lamerei relatives, tends to stay low and multi-branched with age. Grow it in a mineral, fast-draining succulent mix and water only once the soil has dried completely, cutting back almost entirely during its winter leaf-drop rest. Full sun and warm temperatures keep growth compact and the caudex well-formed, while low light or cool damp conditions invite stem rot. Handle it carefully when repotting, since like other pachypodiums the stems carry irritant sap and sharp spines.

planting.note: Sow seed in spring warmth around 72-77F and only move seedlings outdoors once nights stay well above 50F.

directions: Native to the spiny forest of southern Madagascar, this tree grows tall, thorn-studded upright stems bearing small, rounded, deciduous leaves that drop during dry spells, giving it a stark, candelabra-like silhouette. It wants intense sun and a gritty, sharply draining mix, with soil allowed to dry out fully between waterings since it stores moisture in its succulent stems. In frost-free climates it can be planted in the ground, but anywhere with winter chill it needs container culture and a bright, dry indoor spot once temperatures drop. Its stems are lined with stiff spines, so site it away from paths and handle it with thick gloves.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm, bright conditions and harden off slowly, since young plants are far more cold-sensitive than mature specimens.

directions: The tallest of the Madagascar spiny-forest Alluaudia, this species develops a thick, often leaning or arching trunk armed with paired spines and small succulent leaves that it sheds in dry periods. It needs the same lean, mineral, fast-draining soil and full, unobstructed sun that its native spiny thicket habitat provides, with watering reserved for when the root zone has gone fully dry. Growth is slow for the first few years while the trunk thickens, after which height increases more noticeably in warm, humid summer weather. Because mature plants carry substantial spines, give it generous clearance from walkways in frost-free landscape plantings.

planting.note: Germinate seed in warm, humid conditions, then shift seedlings to a lean, fast-draining mix as soon as they establish true leaves.

directions: This Didiereaceae endemic of Madagascar's dry south grows a single, densely spine-covered columnar trunk that branches with age into an upright candelabra form, bearing small succulent leaves that flush after rain and drop in dry periods. It is slower and more cold-sensitive than the related Alluaudia and demands a mineral, very fast-draining soil along with intense sun to avoid etiolated, weak growth. Water sparingly and only once the soil is completely dry, since this species is especially prone to rot in cool or soggy conditions. Grow it in a container where winters are not reliably frost-free, moving it to a bright, dry spot for the cold months.

planting.note: Let cuttings callus for several days before setting in dry, gritty mix, and withhold water until new roots have formed.

directions: Known in the succulent trade as silver thicket, this Madagascar euphorbia forms a dense, tangled mass of grey-green, spine-lined branchlets that give mature plants a distinctive thorny, shrubby silhouette quite unlike the more commonly grown candelabra-type euphorbias. It thrives in intense sun and a mineral, sharply draining substrate, with soil left to dry fully between waterings since overwatering quickly causes branch and root rot. Because its milky latex sap is a skin and eye irritant, wear gloves and eye protection when pruning or propagating from stem cuttings. Keep it frost-free year round, bringing container specimens indoors to a bright window whenever temperatures threaten to drop near freezing.

planting.note: Pot bare-root or nursery-grown specimens into a lean, fast-draining mix only once warm, settled weather has arrived.

directions: Prized in the caudiciform and bonsai succulent trade as the elephant tree, this Madagascar native develops a swollen, gnarled grey trunk and surface roots topped by sprays of small, glossy, pinnate leaflets that give it a miniature-tree appearance even in a shallow pot. It grows best in full sun with a very fast-draining mineral mix, taking regular water while actively leafed out in warm weather but needing a much drier regimen through its winter dormancy when leaves may drop entirely. Its slow, naturally gnarled growth and tolerance of root restriction make it a favorite for shallow bonsai-style containers, where careful shaping over years exaggerates the twisting trunk form. Keep it well above freezing at all times, since cold combined with wet soil is the most common cause of trunk rot.

planting.note: Divide or pot up offsets and bulbils in spring once the soil has warmed, since this species produces plantlets along its flowering stems rather than relying only on seed.

directions: This Madagascar aloe forms clumping rosettes of narrow, often mottled green leaves and takes its name from the small bulbil plantlets it produces along its inflorescences, an unusual propagation habit among aloes that lets clumps spread readily once established. It prefers bright, full sun and a gritty, fast-draining soil, with watering reserved for when the mix has dried out, since like most Madagascar aloes it is intolerant of standing moisture around its roots. Clumps offset steadily with age, and the bulbils can be detached and rooted separately once they develop their own small root systems. Protect it from any frost and keep it on the drier side through winter to avoid rot.
